connector: You have read the whole biography, from a little girl asking Daddy Ben about the star “that never moves” to the last page, where the North Star shines again. Today, say in one sentence what the whole book is about, then test it against the beginning, the middle, and the end.

plate.alt: Daddy Ben points out the North Star to young Harriet outside a cabin in Maryland.
plate.credit: From Chapter 1. The same star shines on the book’s last page.

a.raw: from her wheelchair harriet sang songs about the war
a.fixed: From her wheelchair Harriet sang songs about the war.
a.why: Capital F starts the sentence; capital H on Harriet; a period ends it. From her wheelchair and about the war are prepositional phrases.

b.raw: at dusk the north star shone in the darkening sky
b.fixed: At dusk the North Star shone in the darkening sky.
b.why: Capital A starts the sentence; capital N and S on North Star (the name of one star); a period ends it. At dusk and in the darkening sky are prepositional phrases.

notes.wordParts: pens = pay or weigh out, fid = trust, leg/lect = choose or gather: pension, confident, legend, elect.
notes.grammar: Editing day. Cut the prepositional phrases the reader doesn’t need, then read it aloud. You should hear the verb again.
notes.spelling: Four suffix rules, one year: double the last consonant after a short vowel (run → running), drop the silent e (hope → hoping), and change y to i (happy → happiest, carry → carried). Look at the end of the base word first.

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. You finished Freedom Train. That’s a whole life, from a little girl asking about a star to a woman the whole country knew. Today’s question: what does Harriet’s life mean, taken all together?
transcripts.read: Today you flip back, not forward. Find one moment from the beginning, one from the middle, and one from the end. Check that all three point to the same big idea. If they don’t, maybe your idea needs to grow. Then hold Chapter 1 and the last page side by side.
transcripts.grammar: Last grammar job: the editor’s cut. Some sentences pile up so many little phrases that the action gets buried. Keep the ones the reader needs. Cut the rest. Then read it out loud. You should hear the verb again.

virtue.title: The freedom meter
virtue.moment: A little girl asks Daddy Ben about the star “that never moves.” Years later she crosses into Maryland nineteen times, guides the gunboats up the Combahee, and tells the women working for the vote to “stand together.” On the last page, the North Star is shining again.
virtue.ask: How much did Harriet change the world around her? Slide to show.
virtue.placeholder: Harriet changed the world this much because…
virtue.take: One way to see it: when William Still told her to stay safe, she said, “I must go down, like Moses into Egypt, to lead them out.” She kept going down for the rest of her life.
virtue.name: freedom
